beast-shengsheng.quote: It resembles an ape with white ears. It crouches and walks as a person does. Its name is Shengsheng.

beast-lushu.quote: It resembles a horse with a white head, tiger markings and a red tail. Its cry is like singing. It is called Lushu; wearing it is said to favor descendants.

beast-jiuweihu.quote: It resembles a fox with nine tails. Its cry is like an infant's. It can eat people; eating it is said to protect against harmful influences.

beast-chiru.quote: It resembles a fish with a human face and a mandarin duck's call. Eating it is said to prevent scabies.

beast-boyi.quote: It resembles a goat with nine tails, four ears and eyes on its back. Its name is Boyi; wearing it is said to dispel fear.

beast-xuangui.quote: It resembles a turtle with a bird's head and a serpent's tail. Its cry is like splitting wood. Wearing it is said to prevent deafness.

beast-gudiao.quote: It resembles an eagle with horns. Its cry is like an infant's, and it eats people.

beast-tian-gou.quote: It resembles a wildcat with a white head and is called Tiangou. Its cry is liuliu; it can ward off calamity.

beast-bifang.quote: It resembles a crane with one leg, red markings, a blue-green body and a white beak. Its appearance foretells fire in the settlement.

beast-zheng.quote: It resembles a red leopard with five tails and one horn. Its cry is like striking stone. Its name is Zheng.

beast-qiongqi-hainei.quote: Qiongqi resembles a winged tiger. It eats people beginning at the head; those it eats wear their hair loose.

beast-qiongqi-xishan.quote: It resembles an ox with hedgehog spines. Its cry is like a howling dog.

beast-dangkang.quote: It resembles a pig with tusks. Its name is Dangkang, and its cry calls its own name.

beast-zhuyan.quote: It resembles an ape with a white head and red feet. Its name is Zhuyan; its appearance foretells great warfare.

beast-yingzhao.quote: The deity has a horse's body, human face, tiger markings and bird's wings. It patrols the four seas; its cry is like liu.

beast-luwu.quote: The deity has a tiger's body and nine tails, a human face and tiger's claws. It oversees heaven's nine divisions and the seasons of the ruler's gardens.

beast-tulou.quote: It resembles a goat with four horns. Its name is Tulou, and it eats people.

beast-qinyuan.quote: It resembles a bee, as large as a mandarin duck. Its name is Qinyuan. Animals it stings die; trees it stings wither.

beast-wenyaoyu.quote: There are many Wenyaoyu, resembling carp with fish bodies and bird's wings, blue-green markings, white heads and red beaks. They range through the Western Sea and swim in the Eastern Sea, flying at night. Their cry resembles the luan bird; their appearance foretells abundant harvests throughout the land.

beast-guan.quote: A beast there resembles a wildcat, with one eye and three tails. Its name is Huan; its cry overpowers a hundred voices and can ward off calamity.

beast-bo.quote: It resembles a horse with a single patterned horn. Its name is Bo, and it can ward off warfare.

beast-jingwei.quote: It resembles a crow, with a patterned head, white beak and red feet. Its name is Jingwei, and its cry speaks its own name. It constantly carries wood and stones from the western mountains to fill the Eastern Sea.

beast-fei.quote: It resembles an ox with a white head, one eye and a serpent's tail. Its name is Fei. Water dries where it walks; grass dies where it treads. Its appearance foretells great pestilence.

beast-zhu-jian.quote: It resembles a leopard with a long tail, human head, ox's ears and one eye. Its name is Zhujian. It roars loudly, holding its tail in its mouth when walking and coiling it when resting.

beast-qiangliang.quote: A deity holds snakes in its mouth and hands. It has a tiger's head and human body, four hooves and long elbows. Its name is Qiangliang.

beast-zhulong.quote: Beyond the northwestern sea, north of the Red River, stands Mount Zhangwei. Its deity has a human face and red serpent's body, with straight eyes. Darkness falls when its eyes close; light returns when they open. It neither eats, sleeps nor breathes, and calls forth wind and rain. It is Zhu Jiuyin, also called Zhulong.

beast-xiangliu.quote: Gonggong's retainer is named Xiangliu. He has nine heads and feeds upon nine mountains.

beast-kaiming.quote: Kunlun's Kaiming beast has a large tiger-like body and nine heads, all with human faces. It stands facing east upon Kunlun.

beast-dijiang.quote: It resembles a yellow sack, red as cinnabar fire, with six feet and four wings, formless and without a face or eyes.

beast-luoyu.quote: It resembles a fish with bird's wings. Its cry is like a mandarin duck's; its appearance foretells flooding in the settlement.

beast-phoenix.quote: A bird there resembles a chicken with five-colored markings. Its name is Fenghuang. The marking on its head is called virtue; on its wings, righteousness; on its back, ritual propriety; on its chest, benevolence; on its belly, trustworthiness.

beast-heyu.quote: A beast there resembles a pig with a human face, yellow body and red tail. Its name is Heyu, and its cry is like an infant's.

01-01.source_text: Sanwu Liji, Xu Zheng (Three Kingdoms, Wu); surviving passages quoted in Yiwen Leiju, vol. 1, and Taiping Yulan, vol. 2.
01-01.source_quote: Heaven and earth were a chaos like an egg, and Pangu was born within it. After eighteen thousand years they separated: the clear yang became heaven and the turbid yin became earth. Between them Pangu changed nine times each day, divine in heaven and sage upon earth. Each day heaven rose one zhang, earth thickened one zhang and Pangu grew one zhang. After another eighteen thousand years, heaven was exceedingly high, earth exceedingly deep and Pangu exceedingly tall.

01-02.source_text: Fengsu Tongyi, Huangba, vol. 1, Ying Shao (Eastern Han); in Wang Liqi's annotated edition.
01-02.source_quote: When heaven and earth had opened, there were no people. Nuwa kneaded yellow earth to make them. The task was too great for her strength, so she drew a cord through mud and lifted it to make people.

01-03.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03.source_quote: In ancient times the four supports failed and the Nine Regions split. Heaven did not cover everything, nor did earth support everything. Fire burned without end and water surged without cease; fierce beasts devoured people and birds of prey seized the old and weak. Nuwa smelted five-colored stones to repair the sky, cut off a giant turtle's legs to raise the four supports, killed the black dragon to save Jizhou, and piled reed ash to stop the flood.

01-03-a.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-a.source_quote: Nuwa smelted five-colored stones to repair the azure sky.

01-03-b.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-b.source_quote: She cut off the giant turtle's legs to raise the four supports.

01-03-c.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-c.source_quote: She killed the black dragon to save Jizhou.

01-03-d.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-d.source_quote: She piled reed ash to stop the overflowing waters.

01-04.source_text: Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-04.source_quote: Gonggong contended with Zhuanxu for rulership. In anger he struck Mount Buzhou, breaking heaven's pillar and earth's bonds. Heaven tilted northwest, drawing the sun, moon and stars that way; earth sank in the southeast, drawing waters and dust toward it.

02-01.source_text: Zhouyi (Book of Changes), Xici II; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
02-01.source_quote: When Fuxi ruled the world, he looked upward at heaven's patterns and downward at earth's forms. He observed the markings of birds and beasts and the conditions of the land, taking examples nearby from his own body and far away from other things. Thus he first created the eight trigrams to communicate divine powers and classify the nature of all things.

02-02.source_text: Fengsu Tongyi, Ying Shao (Eastern Han); Duyi Zhi, Li Rong (Tang), final volume.
02-02.source_quote: Nuwa was Fuxi's younger sister (Fengsu Tongyi). At the world's beginning only Nuwa and her brother lived on Mount Kunlun. They considered marrying but felt ashamed. They prayed that, if heaven intended their union, the smoke should join; otherwise it should scatter. The smoke joined (Duyi Zhi).
02-02.basis_note: No Shanhaijing place or direction supports this location. The marker indexes a chapter story; it does not identify an actual site or distance.

02-03.source_text: Huainanzi, Xiuwu Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
02-03.source_quote: Shennong tasted the flavors of the many herbs and encountered seventy poisons in a single day.

02-04.source_text: Hanfeizi, Wu Du, Han Fei (Warring States); Wang Xianshen's Hanfeizi Jijie.
02-04.source_quote: In ancient times people were few and beasts many. People ate fruits and shellfish, whose rawness and foul odors harmed their stomachs, and many became ill. A sage appeared who made fire by friction to cook away the rawness. The people rejoiced, made him ruler of the world and called him Suiren.

02-05.source_text: Hanfeizi, Wu Du, Han Fei (Warring States); Wang Xianshen's Hanfeizi Jijie.
02-05.source_quote: In ancient times people were few and beasts many; people could not withstand beasts, insects and snakes. A sage appeared who built wooden nests to escape these dangers. The people rejoiced, made him ruler of the world and called him Youchao.

03-01.source_text: Shiji, Wudi Benji, Sima Qian (Western Han); with the three commentaries.
03-01.source_quote: In Xuanyuan's time, Shennong's lineage declined. He fought the Yan Emperor on the plain of Banquan. After three battles he achieved his purpose.
03-01.basis_note: The Shiji describes the Yellow Emperor fighting the Yan Emperor at Banquan. Modern identifications differ; this marker establishes no candidate site, real direction or distance.

03-02.source_text: Shiji, Wudi Benji, Sima Qian (Western Han); with the three commentaries.
03-02.source_quote: Chiyou rebelled and refused the ruler's commands. The Yellow Emperor summoned the lords' armies and fought Chiyou on the plain of Zhuolu, capturing and killing him.
03-02.basis_note: The Shiji describes the Yellow Emperor fighting Chiyou at Zhuolu. Modern identifications differ; this marker establishes no candidate site, real direction or distance.

03-03.source_text: Shanhaijing, Beyond the Seas: West; Guo Pu commentary edition.
03-03.source_quote: Xingtian contended with the ruler for divine power. The ruler cut off his head and buried it at Mount Changyang. Xingtian then used his nipples as eyes and his navel as a mouth, wielding shield and axe in a dance.
03-03.basis_note: The text names Mount Changyang but provides no verifiable absolute coordinates. This is a narrative anchor.

03-04.source_text: Shanhaijing, Northern Mountains; Guo Pu commentary edition.
03-04.source_quote: Mount Fajiu has many cudrania trees. A bird there resembles a crow, with a patterned head, white beak and red feet. It is called Jingwei, and its cry speaks its own name. It was the Yan Emperor's youngest daughter, Nuwa, who drowned while visiting the Eastern Sea and never returned. She became Jingwei and constantly carried wood and stones from the western mountains to fill the Eastern Sea.
03-04.basis_note: Northern Mountains associates Jingwei with Mount Fajiu and describes carrying western wood and stones to the Eastern Sea. The diagram restates this relationship without absolute distances.
03-04.location_label: Mount Fajiu — Eastern Sea · relationship diagram

03-05.source_text: Shanhaijing, Beyond the Seas: North; Guo Pu commentary edition. Also see Great Wilderness: North.
03-05.source_quote: Kuafu raced after the sun and reached its setting place. Thirsty, he drank from the Yellow and Wei Rivers, but they were insufficient. He went north to drink from the Great Marsh. Before reaching it he died of thirst along the way. His abandoned staff became Deng Forest.
03-05.basis_note: The text describes pursuit, drinking from the two rivers, seeking the Great Marsh, death before arrival and the staff's transformation. Only narrative order is depicted.
03-05.location_label: Yellow and Wei Rivers — Great Marsh · narrative sequence

04-01.source_text: Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
04-01.source_quote: Gonggong contended with Zhuanxu for rulership. In anger he struck Mount Buzhou, breaking heaven's pillar and earth's bonds.
04-01.basis_note: Mount Buzhou has several proposed identifications. This marker aids reading rather than establishing real coordinates.

04-02.source_text: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
04-02.source_quote: In Yao's time ten suns rose together, scorching crops and killing plants, leaving people without food. Yayu, Zaochi, Jiuying, Dafeng, Fengxi and the long serpent harmed the people. Yao sent Yi to kill Zaochi in the wilds of Chouhua, Jiuying above the fierce waters, and Dafeng at Qingqiu's marsh. He shot upward at the ten suns and killed Yayu below, severed the long serpent at Dongting and captured Fengxi in the mulberry grove.
04-02.basis_note: The passage lists several actions and places together. This marker does not identify a single site or reconstruct a route.
04-02.location_label: Actions in several places · relationship diagram

04-03.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
04-03.source_quote: Yi obtained the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West. Heng'e stole it and fled to the moon; he felt bereft and had no way to replace it.
04-03.basis_note: The passage describes a mythical flight to the moon; it is not projected onto earthly coordinates.

04-04.source_text: Shanhaijing, Within the Seas; Guo Pu commentary edition.
04-04.source_quote: Floodwaters reached heaven. Without awaiting the ruler's command, Gun stole the ruler's growing earth to dam the flood. The ruler ordered Zhurong to kill Gun at Yujiao. Gun then brought forth Yu.
04-04.basis_note: The text places Gun's death at Yujiao, whose absolute location cannot be reliably established.

04-05.source_text: Shangshu (Book of Documents), Yao Dian; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
04-05.source_quote: Yao said: 'Shun, heaven's succession now rests upon you. Faithfully hold to the middle way. If the people of the four seas suffer hardship, heaven's favor will end forever.' Shun likewise charged Yu.
04-05.basis_note: The cited entry describes Yao charging Shun, without a specific place or direction suitable for map positioning.

05-01.source_text: Shangshu (Book of Documents), Yu Gong; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
05-01.source_quote: Yu ordered the land, followed the mountains to clear trees, and established the great mountains and rivers.
05-01.basis_note: Flood control involves many waterways. This narrative anchor identifies no single event site, Nine Regions boundary, ancient riverbed or activity area.
05-01.location_label: Flood control in many places · narrative diagram

05-02.source_text: Shanhaijing, Beyond the Seas: North. Also compare Xiangyao in Great Wilderness: North.
05-02.source_quote: Gonggong's retainer Xiangliu had nine heads and fed upon nine mountains. Wherever he went became marshes and streams. Yu killed Xiangliu; his foul blood made the land unfit for grain. Yu tried to fill it, but it repeatedly collapsed, so he made it a terrace for the rulers, north of Kunlun and east of Rouli. Xiangliu had nine human faces and a blue-green serpent's body.
05-02.basis_note: This passage is from Beyond the Seas: North, rather than the Xiangyao entry in Great Wilderness: North. The rulers' terrace is described as north of Kunlun and east of Rouli, but this does not locate the killing or establish modern coordinates. Candidate sites and illustrations are not location evidence.

05-03.source_text: Shangshu (Book of Documents), Yi Ji; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
05-03.source_quote: While engaged in this work, I married at Tushan, on the days xin, ren, gui and jia. Qi cried as a newborn, but I did not attend to him, devoting myself to planning the work on the land.
05-03.basis_note: Modern identifications of Tushan include Huaiyuan, Chongqing and Zhejiang. This anchor selects none of them and establishes no direction or distance relative to other events.

05-04.source_text: Hanshu, Wudi Ji; Yan Shigu's commentary quoting the Huainanzi. This passage is absent from the received Huainanzi.
05-04.source_quote: Yu controlled the flood and opened a way through Mount Huanyuan, transforming into a bear. He told the woman of Tushan to bring food when she heard the drum. Jumping upon a stone, he accidentally struck it. She came, saw him as a bear and fled in shame. At the foot of Mount Songgao she turned to stone while pregnant with Qi. Yu called, 'Give me my son.' The stone split on its north side, and Qi was born.
05-04.basis_note: This account survives in Yan Shigu's commentary, attributed to the Huainanzi, but is absent from its received text. The anchor does not locate the Qimu Stone or reconstruct the mountain.
05-04.location_label: Foot of Mount Songgao · narrative diagram

06-01.source_text: Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xiang, year 4; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
06-01.source_quote: As Xia declined, Houyi moved from Chu to Qiongshi. Relying on Xia's people, he took over its government.

06-02.source_text: Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xiang, year 4; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
06-02.source_quote: Han Zhuo was an unprincipled member of the Boming clan. Rejected by its ruler, he was taken in by Yi, trusted and made minister. Zhuo flattered those within and bribed those outside, deceiving the people while luring Yi into hunting. Through treachery he seized the state and won compliance within and without. Yi remained unrepentant; returning from the hunt, his household killed and cooked him.

06-03.source_text: Zuo Zhuan, Duke Ai, year 1; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
06-03.source_quote: Jiao of Guo destroyed Zhen'guan, attacked Zhenxun and killed Xia's ruler Xiang. His pregnant wife Min escaped through a hole, returned to Youreng and bore Shaokang. As Youreng's official in charge of herds, he remained wary of Jiao. Pursued by Jiao's agent, he fled to Youyu and became chief cook. Yu Si married him to his two daughters and granted him Lun. With a tract of land and a company of followers, he cultivated virtue and planned to rally Xia's people and restore its officials.
06-03.location_label: Youreng, Youyu and Lun · migration narrative

06-04.source_text: Shiji, Xia Benji, Sima Qian (Western Han); with the three commentaries.
06-04.source_quote: Jie of Xia held a gathering at Reng, and Youmin rebelled. Jie defeated Youmin, thereby bringing about his state's ruin. He summoned Tang, imprisoned him at Xiatai and later released him.

06-05.source_text: Lushi Chunqiu, Benwei, Lu Buwei (Warring States), with Gao You's commentary.
06-05.source_quote: A woman of Youshen gathering mulberries found a baby in a hollow mulberry tree and offered him to her ruler, who ordered the cooks to raise him. Investigation revealed that his mother lived beside the Yi River. While pregnant, she dreamed a deity warning: 'When water emerges from the mortar, flee east and do not look back.' The next day water appeared; she warned her neighbors and fled ten li east, then looked back. Her town was submerged, and she became a hollow mulberry tree. Thus the child was named Yi Yin. He grew into a worthy man.

07-03.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 2; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-03.source_quote: The Son of Heaven ascended Kunlun Hill to view the Yellow Emperor's palace and the burial of Fenglong, so that later generations might know of them.
07-03.basis_note: The episode is in volume 2. Modern identifications of Kunlun are disputed. This marker records the narrative rather than a mountain location or real itinerary.

07-01.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 3; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-01.source_quote: On the auspicious jiazi day, the Son of Heaven visited the Queen Mother of the West, presenting a white gui tablet and a dark bi disk.
07-01.basis_note: This episode is in volume 3. Its Queen Mother is not conflated with figures described in different Shanhaijing books. Her country's location is disputed; the layout identifies no real site.

07-02.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 3; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-02.source_quote: On the yichou day the Son of Heaven entertained the Queen Mother beside the Jade Pool. She sang: 'White clouds are in heaven; hills rise below. The way is distant, mountains and rivers divide us. May you live and return again.' He answered: 'I return to the eastern lands to bring peace to the Xia peoples. Once all are at ease, I shall see you again. Within three years I will return to your country.'
07-02.basis_note: The banquet follows the jiazi meeting on the next day, yichou, in volume 3. Identifications of the Jade Pool are disputed. No candidate lake, distance or itinerary is selected.

07-04.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 3; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-04.source_quote: The Son of Heaven ascended Mount Yan, recorded his journey on its stone and planted a scholar tree.
07-04.basis_note: Volume 3 places this episode after the Jade Pool banquet. Mount Yan's location and the following inscription wording are uncertain. The marker selects no modern candidate or route; the illustration invents no inscription.
